stem: Choose the most correct statement containing the parameters which control the size of the target echo.
choices: Transmitted power, antenna effective area, transmit and receive losses, RADAR cross section of the target, range to target.
Height of antenna, power radiated, size of target, receiver gain, pulse width.
Power radiated, antenna gain, size of target, shape of target, pulse width, receiver gain.
Magnetron gain, antenna gain, size of target, range to target, wave-guide loss.
explanation: Echo strength follows the radar range equation: it grows with transmitted power, antenna effective area, and the target's radar cross section, and shrinks with transmit and receive losses and the fourth power of range. Receiver gain only amplifies an echo after it arrives.

stem: Which of the following has NO effect on the maximum range capability?
explanation: Recovery time is how quickly the TR tube and receiver regain full sensitivity after each transmitted pulse, so it limits how close a target can be seen, the minimum range. Carrier frequency, PRF, and receiver sensitivity all affect how far the radar can detect.

stem: What type of transmitter power is measured over a period of time?
explanation: Average power is the peak pulse power spread over the whole repetition period, so it is measured over time: P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>peak</sub> × pulse width × PRF. Peak power is the power during the brief pulse itself.

stem: What RADAR component controls timing throughout the system?
explanation: The synchronizer, also called the timer or trigger generator, produces the timing pulses that fire the modulator and at the same instant start the indicator sweep and range circuits, keeping the whole radar in step.

stem: Which of the following components allows the use of a single antenna for both transmitting and receiving?
explanation: The duplexer switches the antenna between transmitter and receiver: during each pulse it routes energy to the antenna while blocking the receiver, then passes the weak returning echoes to the receiver between pulses.

stem: The sweep frequency of a RADAR indicator is determined by what parameter?
explanation: Each transmitted pulse triggers one sweep on the indicator, so the sweeps repeat at the pulse repetition frequency. Carrier frequency and pulse width have nothing to do with how often the trace restarts.

stem: A radio wave will travel a distance of three nautical miles in:
explanation: A radio wave covers one nautical mile in about 6.17 µs, half of the 12.34 µs radar mile, which is a round trip. One way over three miles: t = 3 × 6.17 µs = 18.51 µs.

stem: One RADAR mile is how many microseconds?
explanation: A radar mile is the time for a pulse to travel out to a target one nautical mile away and back: about 6.17 µs each way, or 12.34 µs in total. Dividing echo time by 12.34 µs gives range in nautical miles.

stem: RADAR range is measured by the constant:
explanation: Radio waves travel about 300 meters per microsecond, but the pulse must go out and come back, so each microsecond of echo delay equals 300 ÷ 2 = 150 meters of range.

stem: If a target is 5 miles away, how long does it take for the RADAR echo to be received back at the antenna?
explanation: Each nautical mile of range takes 12.34 µs for the pulse to go out and return, so t = 5 × 12.34 µs = 61.7 µs.

stem: How long would it take for a RADAR pulse to travel to a target 10 nautical miles away and return to the RADAR receiver?
explanation: A radar mile is 12.34 µs of round-trip time per nautical mile of range: t = 10 × 12.34 µs = 123.4 µs.

stem: What is the distance in nautical miles to a target if it takes 308.5 microseconds for the RADAR pulse to travel from the RADAR antenna to the target and back.
explanation: The 308.5 µs is round-trip time, so divide by the 12.34 µs radar mile: R = 308.5 ÷ 12.34 = 25 nautical miles. Halving the time first would count the return trip twice and give only half the range.

stem: Frequencies generally used for marine RADAR are in the ___ part of the radio spectrum.
explanation: Marine radars operate in the SHF (super high frequency) band, 3 to 30 GHz, mainly S-band near 3 GHz and X-band near 9.4 GHz. These microwave frequencies allow narrow beams from antennas of practical size.

stem: Practical RADAR operation requires the use of microwave frequencies so that:
choices: Stronger target echoes will be produced.
Ground clutter interference will be minimized.
Interference to other communication systems will be eliminated.
Non-directional antennas can be used for both transmitting and receiving.
explanation: At microwave frequencies the wavelength is small compared with ships, buoys, and coastlines, so targets reflect strongly, and a practical-size antenna can form a narrow, high-gain beam that concentrates energy on the target, producing stronger echoes.

stem: An S-band RADAR operates in which frequency band?
explanation: S-band covers 2 to 4 GHz, wavelengths of about 15 down to 7.5 cm. Marine S-band radars typically operate near 3 GHz, a wavelength of roughly 10 cm.

stem: A RADAR operating at a frequency of 3 GHz has a wavelength of approximately:
explanation: λ = c / f = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s ÷ 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> Hz = 0.1 m = 10 cm. That is why S-band radar near 3 GHz is often called 10-centimeter radar.

stem: The major advantage of an S-band RADAR over an X-band RADAR is:
choices: It is less affected by weather conditions.
explanation: The longer S-band wavelength, about 10 cm versus 3 cm, is scattered and absorbed far less by rain, snow, and fog, so S-band sees through bad weather better. X-band, with a narrower beam from the same size antenna, actually has better bearing resolution.

stem: An X band RADAR operates in which frequency band?
explanation: X-band spans 8 to 12 GHz. Marine X-band radars usually transmit near 9.4 GHz, a wavelength of about 3.2 cm.

stem: A pulse RADAR has a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 400 Hz, a pulse width of 1 microsecond, and a peak power of 100 kilowatts. The average power of the RADAR transmitter is:
explanation: Average power equals peak power times duty cycle: P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>pk</sub> × PW × PRF = 100,000 W × 1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 400 Hz = 40 W.

stem: A shipboard RADAR transmitter has a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 1,000 Hz, a pulse width of 0.5 microseconds, peak power of 150 KW, and a minimum range of 75 meters. Its duty cycle is:
explanation: Duty cycle is the fraction of time the transmitter is on: duty cycle = PW × PRF = 0.5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 1,000 Hz = 0.0005. The peak power and minimum range figures are not needed.

stem: A pulse RADAR transmits a 0.5 microsecond RF pulse with a peak power of 100 kilowatts every 1600 microseconds. This RADAR has:
explanation: Average power = peak power × pulse width ÷ pulse period = 100,000 W × 0.5 µs ÷ 1,600 µs = 31.25 W. The PRF is actually 1 ÷ 1,600 µs = 625 Hz, and the duty cycle only 0.03125 percent.

stem: If a RADAR transmitter has a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 900 Hz, a pulse width of 0.5 microseconds and a peak power of 15 kilowatts, what is its average power output?
explanation: P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>pk</sub> × PW × PRF = 15,000 W × 0.5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 900 Hz = 6.75 W. The duty cycle is only 0.00045, so average power is a tiny fraction of peak power.

stem: What is the average power if the RADAR set has a PRF of 1000 Hz, a pulse width of 1 microsecond, and a peak power rating of 100 kilowatts?
explanation: P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>pk</sub> × PW × PRF = 100,000 W × 1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 1,000 Hz = 100 W, which corresponds to a duty cycle of 0.001.

stem: A search RADAR has a pulse width of 1.0 microsecond, a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 900 Hz, and an average power of 18 watts. The unit’s peak power is:
explanation: Rearrange the average-power formula: P<sub>pk</sub> = P<sub>avg</sub> ÷ (PW × PRF) = 18 W ÷ (1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 900 Hz) = 18 ÷ 0.0009 = 20,000 W = 20 kW.

stem: For a range of 5 nautical miles, the RADAR pulse repetition frequency should be:
explanation: Each echo must return before the next pulse fires, so the pulse period must be at least the round-trip time: t = 5 × 12.34 µs = 61.7 µs, and PRF ≤ 1 ÷ 61.7 µs ≈ 16.2 kHz.

stem: For a range of 100 nautical miles, the RADAR pulse repetition frequency should be:
explanation: The echo from 100 nautical miles takes 100 × 12.34 µs = 1,234 µs to return, and the next pulse must wait at least that long: PRF ≤ 1 ÷ 1,234 µs ≈ 810 Hz.

stem: The minimum range of a RADAR is determined by:
choices: The frequency of the RADAR transmitter.
explanation: While the transmitted pulse is on, the receiver is protected and cannot hear echoes, so a target whose echo returns before the pulse ends is masked. Minimum range is about 150 m per microsecond of pulse width.

stem: Short range RADARs would most likely transmit:
choices: Narrow pulses at a fast rate.
Narrow pulses at a slow rate.
Wide pulses at a fast rate.
Wide pulses at a slow rate.
explanation: Narrow pulses give a small minimum range and fine range resolution, and because close-in echoes return quickly, pulses can be sent at a fast repetition rate, which also puts more hits on each target.

stem: For a range of 30 nautical miles, the RADAR pulse repetition frequency should be:
explanation: Round-trip time for 30 nautical miles is 30 × 12.34 µs = 370.2 µs, so the PRF must not exceed 1 ÷ 370.2 µs ≈ 2.7 kHz, or echoes would arrive after the next pulse had fired.

stem: For a range of 10 nautical miles, the RADAR pulse repetition frequency (PRF) should be:
explanation: The echo from 10 nautical miles returns after 10 × 12.34 µs = 123.4 µs, so the maximum PRF is 1 ÷ 123.4 µs ≈ 8.1 kHz. A faster rate would fire the next pulse before distant echoes arrive.

stem: If the PRF is 2500 Hz, what is the PRI?
explanation: The pulse repetition interval is the reciprocal of the PRF: PRI = 1 ÷ PRF = 1 ÷ 2,500 Hz = 0.0004 s = 400 µs.

stem: If the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is 2000 Hz, what is the pulse repetition interval (PRI)?
explanation: PRI = 1 ÷ PRF = 1 ÷ 2,000 Hz = 0.0005 s, or 500 µs, the time from the start of one pulse to the start of the next.

stem: The pulse repetition rate (PRR) refers to:
choices: The reciprocal of the duty cycle.
The pulse rate of the local oscillator tube.
The pulse rate of the klystron.
The pulse rate of the magnetron.
explanation: The pulse repetition rate is how many times per second the magnetron is fired to transmit an RF pulse. The receiver's local oscillator, klystron or solid-state, runs continuously and is not pulsed.

stem: If the RADAR unit has a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 2000 Hz and a pulse width of 0.05 microseconds, what is the duty cycle?
explanation: Duty cycle = PW × PRF = 0.05 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × 2,000 Hz = 0.0001, so the transmitter is on only one ten-thousandth of the time.

stem: Small targets are best detected by:
choices: Short pulses transmitted at a fast rate.
Using a long pulse width with high output power.
All of these answers are correct.
explanation: A small target returns very little energy, so detecting it depends on the energy in each pulse. A long pulse at high output power puts more energy on the target and produces an echo strong enough to stand out above receiver noise.

stem: What is the relationship between pulse repetition rate and pulse width?
choices: Higher PRR with wider pulse width.
The pulse repetition rate does not change with the pulse width.
The pulse width does not change with the pulse repetition rate.
Lower PRR with wider pulse width.
explanation: Long-range settings use wider pulses for more energy on target and lower the PRR, both to allow time for distant echoes and to keep the duty cycle and magnetron average power within limits. Short-range settings do the opposite.

stem: What component of a RADAR receiver is represented by block 46 in Fig. 8A1?
explanation: Block 46 sits between the waveguide and the receiver's crystal detector (mixer), which is where the TR box belongs. It fires during the transmitted pulse to protect the crystal and passes weak echoes the rest of the time.

stem: A basic sample-and-hold circuit contains:
choices: An analog switch and an amplifier.
An analog switch, a capacitor, and an amplifier.
An analog multiplexer and a capacitor.
An analog switch, a capacitor, amplifiers and input and output buffers.
explanation: An analog switch connects the signal to a hold capacitor, then opens to freeze the voltage. A buffer amplifier on the input charges the capacitor quickly, and one on the output keeps the load from draining the stored charge.

stem: When comparing a TTL and a CMOS NAND gate:
choices: Both have comparable input power sourcing.
Both employ Schmitt diodes for increased speed capabilities.
explanation: Both gates actively drive their outputs high: standard TTL uses the upper transistor of its totem-pole output, and CMOS uses P-channel MOSFETs. Neither is a three-state device, and their input current requirements differ greatly.

stem: Silicon crystals:
choices: Are very sensitive to static electric charges.
Should be wrapped in lead foil for storage.
explanation: Silicon mixer and detector crystals are fragile point-contact diodes: static discharge can destroy them, they are stored wrapped in lead foil or in shielded holders to keep stray fields off, and they handle only a few milliamps of current.

stem: Which is typical current for a silicon crystal used in a RADAR mixer or detector circuit?
explanation: Radar mixer and detector crystals are delicate point-contact diodes that run at only a few milliamperes; a crystal current of about 3 mA is typical, and much higher currents would burn out the tiny junction.

stem: What component of a RADAR receiver is represented by block 47 in Fig. 8A1?
explanation: Block 47 is fed directly from the magnetron and feeds the AFC mixer, so it must be the RF attenuator, which cuts a small sample of the powerful transmitter output down to a safe level for the AFC crystal.

stem: The basic frequency determining element in a Gunn oscillator is:
choices: The loading of the oscillator by the mixer.
explanation: The Gunn diode supplies the negative resistance that sustains oscillation, but the resonant cavity it is mounted in sets the frequency. Supply voltage and loading only pull the frequency slightly.

stem: Which of the following is not a method of analog-to-digital conversion?
explanation: Delta-sigma, switched-capacitor (charge redistribution), and dual-slope integration are all genuine analog-to-digital conversion techniques. Dynamic range describes the span of signal levels a converter can handle; it is a specification, not a conversion method.

stem: When comparing TTL and CMOS logic families, which of the following is true:
choices: CMOS logic requires a supply voltage of 5 volts ±20%, whereas TTL logic requires 5 volts ±5%.
Unused inputs should be tied high or low as necessary especially in the CMOS family.
At higher operating frequencies, CMOS circuits consume almost as much power as TTL circuits.
When a CMOS input is held low, it sources current into whatever it drives.
explanation: CMOS draws almost no current while static, but every switching transition charges and discharges load capacitance, so its power rises in proportion to switching frequency. At high clock rates CMOS dissipation approaches that of TTL.

stem: The primary operating frequency of a reflex klystron is controlled by the:
choices: Level of voltage on the control grid.
Voltage applied to the cavity grids.
Voltage applied to the repeller plate.
explanation: The physical size of the resonant cavity sets a reflex klystron's main operating frequency, and coarse tuning is done by mechanically changing it. The repeller voltage only fine-tunes the frequency within a narrow range.

stem: A Gunn diode oscillator takes advantage of what effect?
explanation: A Gunn diode has no PN junction. At high fields, electrons in the bulk of the gallium arsenide transfer to a slower energy band, creating a region of negative resistance, so the device relies on both the bulk effect and negative resistance to oscillate.

stem: Fine adjustments of a reflex klystron are accomplished by:
choices: Adjusting the flexible wall of the cavity.
explanation: Changing the repeller voltage changes how long the electron bunches take to return to the cavity, shifting the frequency slightly, so it provides fine tuning and is what AFC circuits adjust. Coarse tuning changes the cavity dimensions mechanically.

stem: Blocking oscillators operate on the formula of:
choices: None of the above are correct.
explanation: A blocking oscillator conducts for one brief pulse, then is held cut off while its timing capacitor discharges through a resistor. That RC time constant, T = RC, sets the off time and therefore the pulse repetition rate.

stem: The block diagram of a typical RADAR system microprocessor is shown in Fig. 8A2. Choose the most correct statement regarding this system.
choices: The ALU is used for address decoding.
The Memory and I/O communicate with peripherals.
The control unit executes arithmetic manipulations.
The internal bus is used simultaneously by all units.
explanation: In Fig. 8A2 the memory and I/O interface is the only block connected to the external memory and I/O bus, so it handles all communication with memory and peripherals. The internal bus is shared and carries one transfer at a time.

stem: The phantastron circuit is capable of:
choices: Preventing saturation of the RADAR receiver.
Being used to control repeller voltage in the AFC system.
Developing a linear ramp voltage when triggered by an external source.
explanation: A phantastron is a triggered, one-shot sweep generator: when fired by an external trigger, its Miller-integrator action produces a very linear ramp voltage whose length can be set precisely, useful for range-marker and delay timing.

stem: The block diagram of a typical RADAR system microprocessor is shown in Fig. 8A2. Choose the most correct statement regarding this system.
choices: The ALU is used for address decoding.
General registers are used for arithmetic manipulations.
Address pointers are contained in the control unit.
explanation: The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) performs arithmetic and logic operations on data from the general registers and the TEMP register, and its result returns over the internal bus. Address decoding and instruction control happen elsewhere.

stem: In the Line-Driver/Coax/Line-receiver circuit shown in Fig. 8A3, what component is represented by the blank box marked "X"?
explanation: Box X terminates the 50 Ω coax at the receiving end. A 51 Ω resistor, the nearest standard value, matches the cable's characteristic impedance and prevents reflections that would distort the fast digital pulses.

stem: Choose the most correct statement:
choices: The magnetron anode is a low voltage circuit.
The anode of the magnetron carries high voltage.
The filament of the magnetron carries dangerous voltages.
The magnetron filament is a low voltage circuit.
explanation: The magnetron anode is grounded and the cathode is pulsed to a high negative voltage. Because the filament heats the cathode and is tied to it, the filament circuit rides at that same high voltage and is dangerous to touch.

stem: In the circuit shown in Fig. 8A4, U5 pins 1 and 4 are high and both are in the reset state. Assume one clock cycle occurs of Clk A followed by one cycle of Clk B. What are the output states of the two D-type flip flops?
explanation: The left flip-flop's Q̄ output is fed back to its own data input, so from reset (Q low, Q̄ high) its first clock edge loads a high and pin 5 goes high. Pin 5 drives the right flip-flop's data input, so its clock edge then sets pin 9 high.

stem: If more light strikes the photodiode in Fig. 8A5, there will be:
choices: There is wrong polarity on the diode.
explanation: The 12 V battery reverse-biases the photodiode, the normal way to operate one, so only a tiny dark current flows. Light creates electron-hole pairs in the junction, so more light means more reverse current through the diode and meter.

stem: In the circuit shown in Fig. 8A6, which of the following is true?
choices: With A and B high, Q<sub>1</sub> is saturated and Q<sub>2</sub> is off.
With either A or B low, Q<sub>1</sub> is saturated and Q<sub>2</sub> is off.
With A and B low, Q<sub>2</sub> is on and Q<sub>4</sub> is off.
With either A or B low, Q<sub>1</sub> is off and Q<sub>2</sub> is on.
explanation: Fig. 8A6 is a TTL NAND gate. A low on either emitter of the multi-emitter Q<sub>1</sub> lets its base current flow out through that emitter, saturating Q<sub>1</sub>; its collector then pulls the base of Q<sub>2</sub> low, so Q<sub>2</sub> turns off and the output goes high.

stem: What is the correct value of R<sub>S</sub> in Fig. 8A7, if the voltage across the LED is 1.9 Volts with 5 Volts applied and If max equals 40 milliamps?
explanation: The series resistor must drop the supply voltage minus the LED voltage at the maximum forward current: R<sub>S</sub> = (5 V − 1.9 V) ÷ 40 mA = 3.1 V ÷ 0.040 amperes = 77.5 Ω ≈ 77 Ω.

stem: The block diagram of a typical RADAR system microprocessor is shown in Fig. 8A2. Choose the most correct statement regarding this system.
choices: The ALU is used for address decoding.
General registers are used for arithmetic manipulations.
The control unit executes arithmetic manipulations.
Address pointers are contained in the general registers.
explanation: The general-register block holds both the data registers and the address registers, so address pointers are kept there. The ALU does arithmetic rather than address decoding, and the control unit decodes instructions rather than doing arithmetic.

stem: You are troubleshooting a component on a printed circuit board in a RADAR system while referencing the Truth Table in Fig. 8A8. What kind of integrated circuit is the component?
explanation: On each low-to-high clock edge, Qn takes the opposite of Dn (a high in gives a low out), which is the behavior of an inverting D-type flip-flop. A high on the active-low output enable forces the high-impedance Z state, making it three-state.

stem: The magnetron is used to:
choices: Generate the output signal at the proper operating frequency.
Determine the shape and width of the transmitted pulses.
explanation: The magnetron is the radar's RF oscillator: when the modulator pulses it with high voltage, it generates the microwave output at the operating frequency. Pulse shape and width come from the modulator, and the repetition rate from the synchronizer.

stem: The purpose of the modulator is to:
choices: Transmit the high voltage pulses to the antenna.
Provide high voltage pulses of the proper shape and width to the magnetron.
Tune the Magnetron to the proper frequency.
explanation: The modulator stores energy and, when triggered, delivers a high-voltage pulse of the correct shape and width to the magnetron, which oscillates for exactly that time. It does not set the repetition rate or tune the magnetron.

stem: Which of the following statements about most modern RADAR transmitter power supplies is false?
choices: High voltage supplies may produce voltages in excess of 5,000 volts AC.
There are usually separate low voltage and high voltage supplies.
Low voltage supplies use switching circuits to deliver multiple voltages.
Low voltage supplies may supply both AC and DC voltages.
explanation: Radar high-voltage supplies deliver DC to charge the modulator, not thousands of volts of AC, so that is the false statement. Separate low- and high-voltage supplies, switching low-voltage supplies with multiple outputs, and low-voltage supplies providing both AC and DC are all normal.

stem: The purpose of the Pulse Forming Network is to:
choices: Act as a low pass filter.
Act as a high pass filter.
Produce a pulse of the correct width.
explanation: The pulse forming network is an artificial transmission line that charges between pulses and then discharges into the magnetron for a fixed time set by its inductors and capacitors, producing a pulse of the correct width. The synchronizer, not the PFN, sets the repetition rate.

stem: The purpose of the Synchronizer is to:
choices: Generate the modulating pulse to the magnetron.
Generate a timing signal that establishes the pulse repetition rate.
Insure that the TR tube conducts at the proper time.
explanation: The synchronizer produces the trigger pulses that fire the modulator and start the display sweep, so it establishes the pulse repetition rate and keeps the system in step. Pulse width comes from the modulator's pulse forming network.

stem: Which of the following is not part of the transmitting system?
explanation: The transmitting system consists of the modulator, its pulse forming network, and the magnetron. A klystron, where one is used in a marine radar, serves as the receiver's local oscillator, not as part of the transmitter.

stem: High voltage is applied to what element of the magnetron?
explanation: The high-voltage pulse goes to the magnetron cathode as a strongly negative voltage, while the anode block stays at ground. This keeps the large external anode and the attached waveguide safe to touch.

stem: The characteristic of the magnetron output pulse that relates to accurate range measurement is its:
explanation: Range is timed from the leading edge of the transmitted pulse, so a fast, sharp rise time gives a precise starting reference. A slow, sloping rise makes the timing point uncertain and degrades range accuracy.

stem: What device is used as a transmitter in a marine RADAR system?
explanation: Marine radars use a magnetron as the transmitter because it efficiently produces high-power microwave pulses from a compact, rugged tube. A klystron served as the receiver's local oscillator in older sets, and a thyratron is a modulator switch.

stem: The magnetron is:
choices: A type of diode that requires an internal magnetic field.
A triode that requires an external magnetic field.
Used as the local oscillator in the RADAR unit.
A type of diode that requires an external magnetic field.
explanation: A magnetron has only two elements, a cathode and an anode block, so it is a diode. A permanent magnet outside the tube supplies the magnetic field that curves the electrons' paths so they excite the resonant cavities.

stem: A negative voltage is commonly applied to the magnetron cathode rather than a positive voltage to the magnetron anode because:
choices: The cathode must be made neutral to force electrons into the drift area.
A positive voltage would tend to nullify or weaken the magnetic field.
The anode can be operated at ground potential for safety reasons.
The cavities might not be shock-excited into oscillation by a positive voltage.
explanation: A negative pulse on the cathode produces the same anode-to-cathode potential as a positive pulse on the anode, but lets the anode block, which is bolted to the waveguide and housing, sit safely at ground potential.

stem: The anode of a magnetron is normally maintained at ground potential:
choices: Because it operates more efficiently that way.
Never. It must be highly positive to attract the electrons.
Because greater peak-power ratings can be achieved.
explanation: The anode block forms the magnetron's outer body and connects to the waveguide and chassis, so it is kept at ground for safety and the high voltage is applied as a negative pulse to the cathode. The anode is still positive relative to the cathode.

stem: In a solid-state RADAR modulator, the duration of the transmitted pulse is determined by:
explanation: In a line-type solid-state modulator, an SCR or similar switch simply discharges the pulse forming network into the pulse transformer. The PFN's inductors and capacitors set how long that discharge lasts, and therefore the transmitted pulse duration; the trigger only starts it.

stem: The modulation frequency of most RADAR systems is between:
explanation: The modulator fires the magnetron once per transmitted pulse, so the modulation frequency is simply the pulse repetition rate. The exam takes the typical range as 60 to 500 Hz, low enough to leave long listening time between pulses for distant echoes.

stem: A shipboard RADAR uses a PFN driving a magnetron cathode through a step-up transformer. This results in which type of modulation?
explanation: The PFN discharges through the step-up transformer to put brief high-voltage pulses on the magnetron cathode, so the magnetron switches fully on and off. RF emitted only in short bursts is pulse modulation.

stem: In a pulse modulated magnetron what device determines the shape and width of the pulse?
explanation: The pulse forming network is an artificial transmission line; when the switch discharges it, its inductors and capacitors determine the width and shape of the high-voltage pulse sent to the magnetron. The thyratron only acts as the switch.

stem: What device(s) may act as the modulator of a RADAR system?
explanation: The modulator's switching element, a hydrogen thyratron in older sets or an SCR in solid-state ones, discharges the PFN to form the drive pulse. The magnetron and klystron are microwave oscillators, and the video amplifier belongs to the receiver.

stem: The purpose of a modulator in the transmitter section of a RADAR is to:
choices: Provide the correct waveform to the transmitter.
explanation: The modulator delivers a high-voltage pulse of the correct amplitude, width, and shape to the magnetron at each trigger, giving the transmitter the waveform it needs. Bearing resolution and sea return depend on the antenna and receiver, not the modulator.

stem: The pulse developed by the modulator may have an amplitude greater than the supply voltage. This is possible by:
choices: Discharging a capacitor through an inductor.
Discharging two capacitors in series and combining their charges.
explanation: A resonant charging choke forms a series resonant circuit with the PFN capacitance; its collapsing magnetic field keeps current flowing after the capacitors reach supply voltage, charging them to nearly twice that voltage. A diode holds the charge until the switch fires.

stem: Pulse transformers and pulse-forming networks are commonly used to shape the microwave energy burst RADAR transmitter. The switching devices most often used in such pulse-forming circuits are:
explanation: The switch that discharges the PFN must withstand high voltage, carry very high peak current, and turn on fast. Hydrogen thyratrons and SCRs are latching switches that turn off once the PFN is discharged, which makes them the usual devices for the job.

stem: The purpose of the pulse-forming network is to:
choices: Determine the width of the modulating pulses.
Act as a high pass filter.
Act as a log pass filter.
explanation: The PFN is an artificial transmission line whose delay sets the pulse duration: when discharged, it delivers a flat-topped pulse lasting twice the line's one-way delay. The synchronizer, not the PFN, sets the repetition rate.

stem: The shape and duration of the high-voltage pulse delivered to the magnetron is established by:
choices: An RC network in the keyer stage.
The duration of the modulator input trigger.
The time required to saturate the pulse transformer.
explanation: The pulse forming network is an artificial delay line of inductors and capacitors. When it discharges, the pulse lasts twice its electrical delay, so its component values fix the shape and duration of the high-voltage pulse sent to the magnetron.

stem: Pulse-forming networks are usually composed of the following:
choices: Resonant circuit with an inductor and capacitor.
explanation: A PFN imitates a transmission line with lumped parts: inductors in series along the line and capacitors shunted to ground, matching a real line's series inductance and shunt capacitance. This ladder delivers a nearly rectangular pulse when discharged.

stem: An artificial transmission line is used for:
choices: Testing the RADAR unit, when actual targets are not available.
Determining the shape and duration of pulses.
Testing the delay time for artificial targets.
explanation: An artificial transmission line, the pulse forming network, stores energy in its LC sections and releases it as a pulse lasting twice its delay time, so it determines the shape and duration of the modulator pulse.

stem: The ferrite material in a circulator is used as a(an):
explanation: In a magnetic field, the ferrite shifts the phase of a wave by different amounts depending on its direction of travel. This nonreciprocal phase shift steers energy around the ports in one direction only: transmitter to antenna, antenna to receiver.

stem: In a circular resonant cavity with flat ends, the E-field and the H-field form with specific relationships. The:
choices: E-lines are parallel to the top and bottom walls.
E-lines are perpendicular to the end walls.
H-lines are perpendicular to the side walls.
H-lines are circular to the end walls.
explanation: In the usual TM<sub>010</sub> mode of a cylindrical cavity, the electric field runs straight between the flat end walls, parallel to the axis and perpendicular to those walls, while the magnetic field forms circles around the axis.

stem: A ferrite circulator is most commonly used in what portion of a RADAR system?
explanation: A ferrite circulator acts as the duplexer: its one-way coupling sends the magnetron's pulse to the antenna and routes incoming echoes from the antenna to the receiver, isolating the receiver from the transmitter.

stem: A circulator provides what function in the RF section of a RADAR system?
choices: It replaces the TR cell and functions as a duplexer.
It cools the magnetron by forcing a flow of circulating air.
It permits tests to be made to the thyristors while in use.
It transmits antenna position to the indicator during operation.
explanation: The circulator's one-way ports send transmitter power to the antenna and returning echoes to the receiver, so it performs the duplexing job otherwise done by TR and ATR tubes. It has nothing to do with cooling, testing, or antenna position.

stem: A directional coupler has an attenuation of -30 db. A measurement of 100 milliwatts at the coupler indicates the power of the line is:
explanation: A −30 dB coupler samples 1/1,000 of the line power, since 10<sup>30/10</sup> = 1,000. The line therefore carries P = 100 mW × 1,000 = 100 W.

stem: What is the purpose or function of the RADAR duplexer/circulator?
choices: An electronic switch that allows the use of one antenna for both transmission and reception.
A coupling device that is used in the transition from a rectangular waveguide to a circular waveguide.
A modified length of waveguide used to sample a portion of the transmitted energy for testing purposes.
A dual section coupling device that allows the use of a magnetron as a transmitter.
explanation: The duplexer or circulator acts as a fast switch: during each pulse it connects the transmitter to the antenna and isolates the receiver, then connects the antenna to the receiver to pick up echoes, so one antenna serves both jobs.

stem: The ATR box:
choices: Protects the receiver from strong RADAR signals.
Prevents the received signal from entering the transmitter.
Turns off the receiver when the transmitter is on.
explanation: The ATR (anti-transmit-receive) box sits in the transmitter branch. Between pulses it is unfired and blocks that branch, so weak echoes go to the receiver instead of being lost into the magnetron. Protecting the receiver is the TR box's job.

stem: When a pulse RADAR is radiating, which elements in the TR box are energized?
choices: Both the TR and ATR tubes.
Neither the TR nor ATR tubes.
explanation: The high-power transmitted pulse ionizes the gas in both tubes: the TR tube fires to short the receiver path and protect it, and the ATR tube fires so the pulse passes freely to the antenna.

stem: The TR box:
choices: Prevents the received signal from entering the transmitter.
Protects the receiver from the strong RADAR pulses.
Turns off the receiver when the transmitter is on.
Protects the receiver from the strong RADAR pulses and mutes the receiver when the transmitter is on.
explanation: The TR tube ionizes during each transmitted pulse, placing a short across the receiver input. This shields the crystal from the high-power pulse and effectively mutes the receiver until the gas deionizes after the pulse.

stem: What device is located between the magnetron and the mixer and prevents received signals from entering the magnetron?
explanation: The ATR tube sits in the transmitter branch, between the magnetron and the junction leading to the mixer. Unfired between pulses, it blocks that branch so received echoes go to the mixer rather than being absorbed by the magnetron.

stem: A keep-alive voltage is applied to:
explanation: A small DC keep-alive voltage maintains a little ionization in the TR tube, so it fires almost instantly when the transmitted pulse arrives and protects the receiver crystal from the leading edge of the pulse.

stem: A DC keep-alive potential:
choices: Is applied to a TR tube to make it more sensitive.
Partially ionizes the gas in a TR tube, making it very sensitive to transmitter pulses.
Fully ionizes the gas in a TR tube.
Is applied to a TR tube to make it more sensitive and partially ionizes the gas in a TR tube.
explanation: The keep-alive electrode maintains a small, partial ionization in the TR tube's gas, which makes the tube far more sensitive so it fires almost instantly when the transmitter pulse arrives. Full ionization all the time would short the receiver and block echoes.

stem: What RADAR circuit determines the pulse repetition rate (PRR)?
explanation: The timer, or synchronizer, generates the trigger pulses that fire the modulator, so it sets how many pulses are transmitted each second, the PRR. It also starts the indicator sweep with each pulse.

stem: The triggering section is also known as the:
explanation: The triggering section is called the synchronizer because its trigger pulses synchronize the modulator, the indicator sweep, and the range-marker circuits so they all start together with each transmitted pulse.

stem: Operation of any RADAR system begins in the:
explanation: Every radar cycle starts with a trigger: the triggering section, or synchronizer, fires the modulator, which drives the magnetron, and at the same moment starts the display sweep. Without the trigger nothing else operates.

stem: The timer circuit:
choices: Provides blanking and unblanking signals for the CRT.
explanation: The timer is the radar's master clock. Besides setting the PRR, it times the range-marker generator and sends the blanking and unblanking gates to the CRT, so all the listed functions belong to it.

stem: Pulse RADARs require precise timing for their operation. Which type circuit below might best be used to provide these accurate timing pulses?
explanation: A single-swing blocking oscillator is a transformer-coupled circuit that fires once and is then cut off by its own RC timing, producing very short, sharp, stable pulses with fast rise times, ideal for precise radar trigger timing.

stem: Unblanking pulses are produced by the timer circuit. Where are they sent?
explanation: Unblanking pulses go to the CRT, turning its electron beam on only during the active sweep so echoes are visible, and leaving the beam blanked during retrace.

stem: An advantage of resonant charging is that it:
choices: Eliminates the need for a reverse current diode.
Reduces the high-voltage power supply requirements.
Maintains a constant magnetron output frequency.
explanation: With resonant charging, a charging choke resonates with the PFN so the PFN charges to nearly twice the DC supply voltage. The supply therefore needs to produce only about half the pulse voltage required.

stem: The characteristics of a field-effect transistor (FET) used in a modern RADAR switching power supply can be compared as follows:
choices: “On” state compares to a bipolar transistor. “Off” state compares to a 1-Megohm resistor.
“On” state compares to a pure resistor. “Off” state compares to a mechanical relay.
“On” state compares to an low resistance inductor. “Off” state compares to a 10-Megohm resistor.
“On” state compares to a resistor. “Off” state compares to a capacitor.
explanation: A MOSFET that is fully on behaves like a small pure resistance, R<sub>DS(on)</sub>, with no junction voltage drop. When off it is essentially an open circuit, like the open contacts of a mechanical relay.

stem: A pulse-width modulator in a switching power supply is used to:
choices: Provide the reference voltage for the regulator.
Vary the frequency of the switching regulator to control the output voltage.
Vary the duty cycle of the regulator switch to control the output voltage.
Compare the reference voltage with the output voltage sample and produce an error voltage.
explanation: The PWM keeps the switching frequency fixed and changes how long the switch is on in each cycle, the duty cycle. A longer on-time delivers more energy per cycle, so varying the duty cycle holds the output voltage constant.

stem: In a fixed-frequency switching power supply, the pulse width of the switching circuit will increase when:
explanation: A lower load impedance draws more current, which tends to pull the output voltage down. The regulator responds by widening the switching pulses to deliver more energy per cycle. Less load current or a rising input or output voltage narrows the pulses instead.

stem: A major consideration for the use of a switching regulator power supply over a linear regulator is:
choices: The switching regulator has better regulation.
The linear regulator does not require a transformer to step down AC line voltages to a usable level.
The switching regulator can be used in nearly all applications requiring regulated voltage.
The overall efficiency of a switching regulator is much higher than a linear power supply.
explanation: A switching regulator's transistor is either fully on or fully off, so it wastes little power and often reaches 80 to 90 percent efficiency or more. A linear regulator burns the excess voltage as heat in its pass transistor, so its efficiency is much lower.

stem: Which of the following characteristics are true of a power MOSFET used in a RADAR switching supply?
choices: Low input impedance; failure mode can be gate punch-through.
High input impedance; failure mode can be gate punch-through.
High input impedance; failure mode can be thermal runaway.
Low input impedance; failure mode can be gate breakdown.
explanation: A power MOSFET's insulated gate gives it very high input impedance, but the thin gate oxide can be punctured by excess gate voltage or static. Unlike bipolar transistors, MOSFETs resist thermal runaway because their on-resistance rises with temperature.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: The front end of the receiver does not provide any amplification to the RADAR signal.
The mixer provides a gain of at least 6 db.
The I.F. amplifier is always a high gain, narrow bandwidth amplifier.
explanation: Marine radar receivers traditionally have no RF amplifier: the echo passes from the duplexer straight to a crystal mixer, which has conversion loss rather than gain. Nearly all amplification happens in the IF strip, and that strip's bandwidth is switched wide or narrow with range, so it is not always narrow.

stem: Logarithmic receivers:
choices: Should not be used in RADAR systems.
explanation: A logarithmic receiver's output rises with the logarithm of the input, compressing an enormous range of echo strengths into a usable output. Strong returns that would drive a linear receiver into saturation still produce distinct, unclipped responses, which is why log receivers suit radar so well.

stem: RADAR receivers are similar to:
explanation: Radar receivers operate at microwave frequencies (X-band near 9.4 GHz, S-band near 3 GHz), using waveguide, a crystal mixer and a microwave local oscillator. That makes them microwave receivers in design, quite unlike FM, HF or TV sets.

stem: What section of the receiving system sends signals to the display system?
explanation: After the second detector recovers the echo pulses, the video amplifier boosts them to the level needed to drive the display. The IF amplifier feeds the detector, not the display, and a radar receiver has no audio stage.

stem: What is the main difference between an analog and a digital receiver?
choices: The presence of decision circuitry to distinguish between “on” and “off” signal levels.
An AGC stage is not required in a digital receiver.
explanation: A digital receiver adds decision circuitry that compares the signal against a threshold and declares each sample on or off (1 or 0). An analog receiver simply passes the continuously varying signal level along without making that decision.

stem: In a RADAR receiver, the RF power amplifier:
explanation: A radar receiver has no RF amplifier stage at all, let alone an RF power amplifier. The weak echo goes from the TR/duplexer directly to the crystal mixer, and gain is provided after conversion by the IF amplifier.

stem: The diagram in Fig. 8C9 shows a simplified RADAR mixer circuit using a crystal diode as the first detector. What is the output of the circuit when no echoes are being received?
explanation: The 60 MHz IF is the difference between the 4155 MHz local oscillator and the 4095 MHz echoes (4155 − 4095 = 60 MHz). With no echoes, the diode sees only the steady LO, which it merely rectifies to DC; nothing exists at 60 MHz for the tuned transformer to pass.

stem: In the receive mode, frequency conversion is generally accomplished by a:
explanation: Radar receivers convert the microwave echo to the IF in a crystal diode mixer, whose nonlinear conduction combines the echo with the local oscillator signal. Pentagrid converter tubes cannot work at microwave frequencies, and waveguide sections or ferrite devices do not mix signals.

stem: An RF mixer has what purpose in a RADAR system?
choices: Mixes the CW transmitter output to form pulsed waves.
Converts a low-level signal to a different frequency.
Prevents microwave oscillations from reaching the antenna.
Combines audio tones with RF to produce the RADAR signal.
explanation: The mixer combines the weak echo with the local oscillator signal to produce a lower intermediate frequency, typically 30 or 60 MHz, that can be amplified easily. It does not form the transmitted pulse or protect the antenna.

stem: In a RADAR unit, the mixer uses a:
explanation: A radar mixer is a semiconductor diode device rather than a tube or transistor stage. The classic element is a silicon point-contact crystal, and newer integrated front ends package PIN diodes with the mixer diodes; the diode's nonlinear conduction combines echo and local oscillator signals into the IF.
flag: Radar mixers use silicon point-contact or Schottky diodes; PIN diodes serve as receiver limiters and switches, not mixers. The pool keys "silicon crystal or PIN diode"; choose it on the exam.

stem: What component of a RADAR receiver is represented by block 49 in Fig. 8A1?
explanation: In Fig. 8A1, block 49 receives a sample of magnetron output through block 47 and the klystron signal from block 48. It is the AFC crystal mixer, producing the difference-frequency IF that feeds the AFC IF amplifier and the discriminator.

stem: In a RADAR unit, the mixer uses:
explanation: Radar mixer front ends use semiconductor diodes: the silicon point-contact crystal is the traditional mixing element, and modern integrated assemblies include PIN diodes as well. Naming only one of the two device types is therefore incomplete.
flag: Radar mixers use silicon point-contact or Schottky diodes; PIN diodes serve as receiver limiters and switches, not mixers. The pool keys "PIN diodes and silicon crystals"; choose it on the exam.

stem: The error voltage from the discriminator is applied to the:
explanation: The discriminator's DC error voltage goes to the reflex klystron's repeller (reflector), because changing the repeller voltage shifts the klystron's frequency electronically. This pulls the local oscillator back to the frequency that produces the correct IF.

stem: In a RADAR unit, the local oscillator is a:
explanation: Classic shipboard radars use a reflex klystron as the local oscillator because it generates low-power microwave energy and can be tuned electronically by its repeller voltage for AFC. A hydrogen thyratron is a switch used in the modulator.

stem: What component of a RADAR receiver is represented by block 48 in Fig. 8A1?
explanation: Block 48 feeds both the main crystal detector and the AFC mixer (block 49), and it receives the correction voltage from the AFC output circuit. That makes it the klystron local oscillator, whose signal mixes with both the echoes and the magnetron sample.

stem: What device(s) could be used as the local oscillator in a RADAR receiver?
explanation: Either a reflex klystron (older sets) or a Gunn diode oscillator (solid-state sets) can generate the low-power microwave signal a radar local oscillator needs, so the answer naming both is complete. A thyratron is a switching tube used in modulators.

stem: The klystron local oscillator is constantly kept on frequency by:
choices: A feedback loop from the crystal detector.
A feedback loop from the TR box.
explanation: The AFC circuit mixes a magnetron sample with the klystron output, checks the resulting IF in a discriminator, and feeds an error voltage to the klystron repeller. This holds the local oscillator on frequency automatically as the magnetron or klystron drifts.

stem: How may the frequency of the klystron be varied?
choices: Small changes can be made by adjusting the anode voltage.
Large changes can be made by adjusting the frequency.
By changing the phasing of the buncher grids
Small changes can be made by adjusting the repeller voltage and large changes can be made by adjusting the size of the resonant cavity.
explanation: A reflex klystron is tuned electronically over a small range by its repeller voltage, which changes the electrons' transit time, and mechanically over a large range by changing the size of its resonant cavity, which sets the basic resonant frequency.

stem: Overcoupling in a RADAR receiver will cause?
choices: Increase the range of the IAGC.
explanation: Excessive coupling between the tuned stages of a high-gain IF strip lets energy feed back from output to input. With so much gain available, that unwanted coupling can drive the amplifier into self-oscillation instead of improving returns or reducing noise.
flag: Overcoupling tuned IF stages normally broadens the response into a double-humped curve; oscillation comes from unwanted feedback, not overcoupling as such. The pool keys oscillations; choose it on the exam.

stem: The usual intermediate frequency of a shipboard RADAR unit is:
explanation: Shipboard radar receivers usually use an intermediate frequency of 30 or 60 MHz, high enough to pass the several-megahertz bandwidth that short pulses need. 455 kHz and 10.7 MHz are standard AM and FM broadcast receiver IFs.

stem: The I.F. Amplifier bandwidth is:
choices: Wide for short ranges and narrow for long ranges.
Wide for long ranges and narrow for short ranges.
explanation: Short ranges use short pulses, whose sharp edges need a wide IF bandwidth to preserve range resolution. Long ranges use long pulses, so a narrower bandwidth is enough and it cuts noise, improving sensitivity for weak distant echoes.

stem: A logarithmic IF amplifier is preferable to a linear IF amplifier in a RADAR receiver because it:
explanation: A logarithmic IF amplifier compresses its output, so both very weak and very strong echoes are handled without saturating. That gives a much greater dynamic range than a linear amplifier, whose output clips on strong returns; its gain and noise figure are not inherently better.

stem: The high-gain IF amplifiers in a RADAR receiver may amplify a 2 microvolt input signal to an output level of 2 volts. This amount of amplification represents a gain of:
explanation: Voltage gain in decibels is 20 times the log of the voltage ratio: G = 20 log(2 V / 2 µV) = 20 log(10⁶) = 20 × 6 = 120 dB.

stem: In a RADAR receiver AGC and IAGC can vary between:
explanation: Radar AGC and instantaneous AGC (IAGC) typically provide a gain-control range of about 20 to 40 dB. That is enough to keep strong echoes from large targets or clutter from saturating the IF strip while leaving full gain for weak returns.

stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
choices: The video amplifier is located between the mixer and the I.F. amplifier.
The video amplifier operates between 60 MHz and 120 Mhz.
The video amplifier is located between the I.F. amplifier and the display system.
The video amplifier is located between the local oscillator and the mixer.
explanation: The signal path runs from mixer to IF amplifier to second detector, then to the video amplifier, which boosts the detected pulses to drive the display. The video amplifier handles baseband pulses, not 60 to 120 MHz signals, and has nothing to do with the local oscillator.

stem: Video amplifiers in pulse RADAR receivers must have a broad bandwidth because:
choices: High frequency sine waves must be amplified.
The RADARs operate at PRFs above 100.
The pulses produced are normally too wide for video amplification.
explanation: Echo pulses leaving the detector are both weak and very short. The video amplifier must raise these weak pulses to display level while keeping their steep edges, and that takes a bandwidth of several megahertz; a narrow amplifier would smear and shrink the small pulses.

stem: In video amplifiers, compensation for the input and output stage capacitances must be accomplished to prevent distorting the video pulses. This compensation is normally accomplished by connecting:
choices: Inductors in parallel with both the input and output capacitances.
Resistances in parallel with both the input and output capacitances.
An inductor in parallel with the input capacitance and an inductor in series with the output capacitance.
An inductor in series with the input capacitance and an inductor in parallel with the output capacitance.
explanation: This is series and shunt peaking. A coil in series with the next stage's input capacitance (series peaking) and a coil in the load branch parallel to the output capacitance (shunt peaking) offset those capacitances at high frequencies, extending the response so pulse edges stay sharp.

stem: Which of the following signals is not usually an input to the video amplifier?
explanation: The resolver carries antenna bearing information to the sweep and deflection circuits, not to the video amplifier. Range marker signals and the brilliance and contrast settings all act on the video signal itself.

stem: Which of the following signals are usually an input to the video amplifier?
explanation: Range markers are mixed with the echo video, and the brilliance and contrast controls set the bias and level of the video sent to the display. All of the listed items are therefore normal inputs to the video amplifier.

stem: The video (second) detector in a pulse modulated RADAR system would most likely use a/an:
explanation: Pulse radar echoes are amplitude-modulated bursts of IF energy, so a simple diode envelope detector recovers the video pulses. Discriminators and ratio detectors are FM detectors and respond to frequency, not amplitude.

stem: The AFC system is used to:
choices: Control the frequency of the magnetron.
Control the frequency of the klystron.
Control the frequency of the incoming pulses.
explanation: AFC keeps the IF correct by retuning the klystron local oscillator to follow the magnetron. The magnetron's frequency is not controlled; it drifts, and the klystron is moved to track it.

stem: A circuit used to develop AFC voltage in a RADAR receiver is called the:
explanation: The discriminator puts out a DC voltage whose polarity and size depend on how far the AFC IF is from its center frequency. That error voltage, amplified, is the AFC voltage applied to the klystron.

stem: In the AFC system, the discriminator compares the frequencies of the:
explanation: A sample of magnetron output is mixed with the klystron signal, and the discriminator checks whether their difference equals the nominal IF. In effect it compares the magnetron and klystron frequencies and produces an error voltage when their spacing is wrong.

stem: An AFC system keeps the receiver tuned to the transmitted signal by varying the frequency of the:
explanation: The magnetron cannot practically be retuned in operation, so AFC shifts the local oscillator (klystron) to follow magnetron drift. Keeping the LO a fixed IF away from the transmitter keeps the receiver tuned to the echoes.

stem: A RADAR transmitter is operating on 3.0 GHz and the reflex klystron local oscillator, operating at 3.060 GHz, develops a 60 MHz IF. If the magnetron drifts higher in frequency, the AFC system must cause the klystron repeller plate to become:
explanation: With the LO above the transmitter, IF = 3.060 GHz − 3.000 GHz = 60 MHz. If the magnetron drifts higher, the IF shrinks, so the klystron must also move higher. Making a reflex klystron's repeller more negative returns the electrons sooner and raises its frequency.

stem: What component is block 50 in Fig. 8A1?
explanation: In Fig. 8A1, block 50 sits between the AFC IF amplifier and the AFC output circuit. It is the discriminator, which converts any deviation of the AFC IF from its center frequency into a correction voltage for the klystron.

stem: The STC circuit is used to:
choices: Decrease sea return on a RADAR receiver.
explanation: Sensitivity time control cuts receiver gain right after each transmitted pulse and lets it recover with time. Strong sea return from nearby waves is suppressed, while weaker distant echoes still get full gain.

stem: The STC circuit:
choices: Increases the sensitivity of the receiver for close targets.
Decreases sea return on the PPI scope.
Helps to increase the bearing resolution of targets.
Increases sea return on the PPI scope.
explanation: STC lowers receiver gain immediately after the transmitted pulse, when strong echoes from nearby waves arrive, then restores gain for longer ranges. This reduces the sea clutter around the center of the PPI without affecting bearing resolution.

stem: Sea return is:
choices: Sea water that gets into the antenna system.
The return echo from a target at sea.
The reflection of RADAR signals from nearby waves.
explanation: Sea return, or sea clutter, is radar energy reflected from waves close to the ship. It shows as a cluttered area around the center of the display, strongest at short range and in rough seas.

stem: Sea clutter on the RADAR scope cannot be effectively reduced using front panel controls. What circuit would you suspect is faulty?
explanation: Sea clutter is suppressed by the sensitivity time control circuit, adjusted with the front-panel sea clutter (anti-clutter sea) control. If that control has no effect, suspect the STC circuit; FTC deals with rain clutter, not sea return.

stem: What circuit controls the suppression of sea clutter?
explanation: The STC (sensitivity time control) circuit, set by the sea clutter control, reduces gain for short-range returns where wave echoes are strongest. The EBL, local oscillator and audio stages play no part in clutter suppression.

stem: The sensitivity time control (STC) circuit:
choices: Decreases the sensitivity of the receiver for close objects.
Increases the sensitivity of the receiver for close objects.
Increases the sensitivity of the receiver for distant objects.
Decreases the sensitivity of the transmitter for close objects.
explanation: STC reduces receiver sensitivity immediately after each transmitted pulse, when echoes from close objects and nearby waves arrive, then lets the gain rise with time. It acts on the receiver, never on the transmitter.

stem: Prior to making “power-on” measurements on a switching power supply, you should be familiar with the supply because of the following:
choices: You need to know where the filter capacitors are so they can be discharged.
If it does not use a line isolation transformer you may destroy the supply with grounded test equipment.
It is not possible to cause a component failure by using ungrounded test equipment.
So that measurements can be made without referring to the schematic.
explanation: Many switching supplies rectify the AC line directly, with no isolation transformer, so their circuit common can sit at line potential. Clipping a grounded oscilloscope's ground lead there can short the line and destroy parts, so know the supply's design before taking live measurements.

stem: A constant frequency switching power supply regulator with an input voltage of 165 volts DC, and a switching frequency of 20 kHz, has an “ON” time of 27 microseconds when supplying 1 ampere to its load. What is the output voltage across the load?
choices: It cannot be determined with the information given.
explanation: Output equals input times duty cycle. T = 1 / 20 kHz = 50 µs; duty cycle = 27 µs / 50 µs = 0.54; V<sub>out</sub> = 0.54 × 165 V = 89.1 V DC. The 1-ampere load current does not enter the calculation.

stem: The circuit shown in Fig. 8C10 is the output of a switching power supply. Measuring from the junction of CR6, CR7 and L1 to ground with an oscilloscope, what waveform would you expect to see?
choices: Pulsating DC much higher than line frequency.
explanation: CR6 and CR7 rectify the secondary of T1, which Q1 drives at the high switching frequency. Ahead of the L1 and C6 filter, that junction carries rectified pulses at the switching rate, far above the 60 Hz line frequency.

stem: With regard to the comparator shown in Fig. 8C11, the input is a sinusoid. Nominal high level output of the comparator is 4.5 volts. Choose the most correct statement regarding the input and output.
choices: The leading edge of the output waveform occurs 180 degrees after positive zero crossing of the input waveform.
The rising edge of the output waveform trails the positive zero crossing of the input waveform by 45 degrees.
The rising edge of the output waveform trails the negative zero crossing of the input waveform by 45 degrees.
The rising edge of the output waveform trails the positive peak of the input waveform by 45 degrees.
explanation: The sine drives the inverting input, so the output goes high only after the input falls below the lower trip point of about −1.285 V. That happens just past the negative-going zero crossing, about 180° after the positive zero crossing (slightly more, because of the small hysteresis).

stem: When monitoring the gate voltage of a power MOSFET in the switching power supply of a modern RADAR, you would expect to see the gate voltage change from “low” to “high” by how much?
explanation: A power MOSFET has a gate threshold of roughly 2 to 4 V and needs well above that, typically about 10 V, to switch fully on with low resistance. The gate therefore swings by more than 2 volts between low and high.

stem: The nominal output high of the comparator shown in Fig. 8C11 is 4.5 volts. Choose the most correct statement which describes the trip points.
choices: Upper trip point is 4.5 volts. Lower trip point is approximately 0 volts.
Upper trip point is 2.5 volts. Lower trip point is approximately 2.0 volts.
Upper trip point is 900 microvolts. Lower trip point is approximately 0 volts.
Upper trip point is +1.285 volts. Lower trip point is -1.285 volts.
explanation: Fig. 8C11 is an inverting Schmitt trigger: the 5 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider feeds part of the output back to the noninverting input. With the output swinging ±4.5 V, V<sub>trip</sub> = ±4.5 × 2k / (5k + 2k) = ±1.2857 V ≈ ±1.285 V.

stem: One of the best methods of reducing noise in a RADAR receiver is?
explanation: Isolating the receiver through shielding, physical separation and decoupling of power and signal leads keeps noise from the modulator, transmitter and other shipboard equipment out of its sensitive front end. Changing the frequency or the IF strip does not remove the noise source.

stem: The primary cause of noise in a RADAR receiver can be attributed to:
choices: Thermal noise caused by RADAR receiver components.
explanation: The dominant noise in a radar receiver is thermal noise from random electron motion in its own components, especially the mixer and first IF stages. It sets the receiver's noise figure and limits how weak an echo can be detected.

stem: Noise can appear on the LCD as:
choices: Erratic video and sharp changes in intensity.
explanation: Noise is random, so on an LCD it shows as erratic video speckle with sudden, sharp changes in intensity, rather than as fixed black spots or shifts in target bearing.

stem: RADAR interference on a communications receiver appears as:
explanation: A radar transmits pulses at a fixed repetition rate, so a nearby communications receiver hears them as a steady tone or buzz at the PRF. Its pitch stays constant, unlike random static or hiss.

stem: In a RADAR receiver the most common types of interference are?
explanation: Echoes from rain or snow (weather clutter) and from waves near the ship (sea return) are the most common unwanted returns on a marine radar. They are countered by the FTC rain control and the STC sea control.

stem: Noise can:
explanation: Echoes from small targets can be as weak as the receiver's own noise, so they get lost in it. Large targets return strong echoes that stand well above the noise, and noise does not alter bearings.

stem: The purpose of the discriminator circuit in a RADAR set is to:
choices: Discriminate against two objects with very similar bearings.
Generate a corrective voltage for controlling the frequency of the klystron local oscillator.
Demodulate or remove the intelligence from the FM signal.
explanation: The radar discriminator is part of the AFC loop: it senses how far the AFC IF is from its center frequency and produces a corrective voltage that retunes the klystron local oscillator. It does not separate targets or demodulate an FM signal.

stem: The MTI circuit:
choices: Acts as a mixer in a RADAR receiver.
Is a filter, which blocks out stationary targets, allowing only moving targets to be detected.
Is used to monitor transmitter interference.
Will pick up targets, which are not in motion.
explanation: Moving target indication compares successive echoes and cancels those that are unchanged from pulse to pulse. Stationary targets and clutter are thereby blocked, while moving targets, whose echoes change because of Doppler shift, pass through to the display.

stem: Where is a RF attenuator used in a RADAR unit?
choices: Between the antenna and the receiver.
Between the magnetron and the antenna.
Between the magnetron and the AFC section of the receiver.
Between the AFC section and the klystron.
explanation: The AFC section needs only a tiny sample of the magnetron's high-power output, so an RF attenuator sits between the magnetron and the AFC mixer (block 47 in Fig. 8A1), reducing the sample to a level the crystal can safely handle.

stem: The condition known as “glint” refers to a shifting of clutter with each RADAR pulse and can be caused by a:
explanation: In MTI processing, stationary clutter should cancel identically from one pulse to the next. When the MTI filter is not functioning properly, the clutter residue shifts with each pulse, producing the glint effect.

stem: An ion discharge (TR) cell is used to:
choices: Protect the transmitter from high SWRs.
Lower the noise figure of the receiver.
Tune the local oscillator of the RADAR receiver.
Protect the receiver mixer during the transmit pulse.
explanation: The TR (transmit-receive) cell ionizes during the transmit pulse, shorting the receiver path so the magnetron's high power cannot burn out the sensitive crystal mixer. After the pulse it deionizes and passes the weak echoes to the receiver.

stem: When the receiver employs an MTI circuit:
choices: The receiver gain increases with time.
Only moving targets will be displayed.
The receiver AGC circuits are disabled.
Ground clutter will be free of “rabbits.”
explanation: An MTI receiver cancels echoes that are unchanged from pulse to pulse, so fixed objects and ground clutter disappear. Only targets whose echoes change because of motion (Doppler shift) remain on the display.

stem: Modern liquid crystal displays have a pixel count of:
choices: Can have no more than 125 pixels per inch.
explanation: Current LCD technology routinely exceeds 200 pixels per inch, with phones and tablets commonly at 300 ppi or more, so limits of 50 or 125 ppi understate what modern panels achieve.

stem: Voltages used in CRT anode circuits are in what range of value?
explanation: A CRT's final anode needs a very high accelerating voltage, typically 10 to 50 kV (about 17 kV in many radar displays), to give the beam enough energy for a bright trace. Millivolts or a few hundred volts are far too low.

stem: The purpose of the aquadag coating on the CRT is:
choices: To protect the electrons from strong electric fields.
To act as a second anode.
To attract secondary emissions from the CRT screen.
explanation: The conductive graphite aquadag coating inside the bulb connects to the high-voltage anode. It therefore acts as a second anode, shields the electron beam from stray electric fields and collects secondary electrons knocked off the screen, so all of the listed items apply.

stem: LCD patterns are formed when:
choices: Current passes through the crystal causing them to align.
When voltage is reduced to the raster scan display.
When the deflection coils are resonant.
When the ships antenna’s bearing is true North.
explanation: Energizing a liquid crystal cell makes its molecules align with the applied drive, changing how the cell passes polarized light; selected cells darken or lighten to form the pattern. Deflection coils and antenna bearing play no part in an LCD.

stem: In a raster-type display, the electron beam is scanned:
choices: From the center of the display to the outer edges.
Horizontally and vertically across the CRT face.
In a rotating pattern which follows the antenna position.
From one specified X-Y coordinate to the next.
explanation: A raster display builds the picture like a TV: the beam sweeps horizontally line by line while stepping vertically down the screen. Radial sweeps rotating with the antenna belong to a conventional PPI, and point-to-point X-Y movement is a stroke display.

stem: Select the statement, which is most correct regarding a raster scan display.
choices: Raster displays are the same as conventional T.V. receivers.
The scan rate for a RADAR system is 30 frames per second.
Raster scanning is controlled by clock pulses and requires an address bus.
Raster scanning is not used in RADAR systems.
explanation: In a raster-scan radar, echo data is held in video memory. Clock pulses step the scan while an address bus selects which memory location is read for each pixel. Radar raster displays are not simply TV receivers, and their frame rate is not fixed at 30 per second.

stem: What are the usual input signals to the video amplifier?
explanation: The video amplifier combines the low-level echo video with the fixed range rings and the variable range ring into one composite signal for the display, so all of the listed items are its usual inputs.

stem: Which of the following would not normally be an input to the video amplifier?
explanation: The resolver supplies antenna bearing information to the sweep and deflection circuits, not to the video amplifier. Low-level video and the fixed and variable range rings are all mixed in the video amplifier.

stem: The purpose of the sweep amplifier is to:
choices: Increase the power of the video amplifier.
explanation: The sweep amplifier boosts the sweep generator's sawtooth drive to the current the CRT deflection coils need, producing the radial trace. It does not drive the resolver or add power to the video stage.

stem: How many deflection coils are driven by the sweep amplifier?
explanation: The sweep amplifier drives two deflection coils, one for X (horizontal) and one for Y (vertical) deflection. Feeding them sweep currents weighted by the sine and cosine of antenna bearing makes the trace rotate in step with the antenna.

stem: The main purpose of the sweep generator is to provide:
choices: Composite video to the cathode of the CRT.
The drive signal to the sweep amplifier.
explanation: The sweep generator, triggered by the synchronizer, produces the sawtooth waveform that the sweep amplifier boosts to drive the deflection coils. Range rings and composite video come from other circuits.

stem: The main purpose of the video amplifier is to provide:
choices: Composite video to the cathode of the CRT.
Provide the drive signal to the sweep amplifier.
explanation: The video amplifier combines echo video with the range rings and sends this composite video to the CRT cathode, where it varies beam intensity so targets show as bright spots. Sweep drive and resolver signals are handled elsewhere.

stem: Timing circuits are used to provide what function?
choices: Develop synchronizing pulses for the transmitter system.
Synchronize the antenna and display system.
explanation: Timing circuits produce the synchronizing trigger pulses that fire the modulator and transmitter at the pulse repetition frequency and start the display sweep at the same instant, so every range measurement begins at transmission.

stem: The circuit that develops timing signals is called the:
explanation: The synchronizer, or timer, generates the master timing pulses that trigger the modulator, start the sweep and time the range markers. The pulse forming network only shapes the modulator's high-voltage pulse.

stem: Which of the following functions is not affected by the timing circuit?
explanation: The resolver's output follows the antenna's rotation, not the timing pulses. The timing circuit sets the pulse repetition frequency, triggers the modulator and starts the sweep drive.

stem: The synchronizer primarily affects the following circuit or function:
explanation: The synchronizer's main job is to trigger the modulator, which fires the magnetron at the pulse repetition frequency. Its pulses also start the display sweep, keeping transmission and display in step.

stem: The output from the synchronizer usually consists of a:
explanation: A synchronizer outputs sharp trigger pulses, or square waves from which they are derived, at the pulse repetition rate, because its job is to mark exact instants for the modulator and sweep to start.

stem: The sweep drive is initiated by what circuit?
explanation: The synchronizer's trigger pulse starts the sweep generator at the instant the transmitter fires, so the sweep begins at zero range. The sweep amplifier only amplifies the drive once it has been started.

stem: Accurate range markers must be developed using very narrow pulses. A circuit that could be used to provide these high-quality pulses for the CRT is a:
explanation: A blocking oscillator produces very narrow, steep-sided pulses with fast rise times, which is exactly what sharp, accurately placed range marks on the CRT require.

stem: Range markers are determined by:
explanation: Range markers are generated by the timer (synchronizer) circuits, which produce marker pulses at fixed time intervals after each transmitted pulse, each interval corresponding to the ring spacing. The CRT only displays them.

stem: A gated LC oscillator, operating at 27 kHz, is being used to develop range markers. If each cycle is converted to a range mark, the range between markers will be:
explanation: Each oscillator cycle becomes one range mark. T = 1 / 27 kHz = 37.04 µs; range = 37.04 µs ÷ 12.34 µs per nautical mile ≈ 3.0 nautical miles between markers.

stem: What would be the frequency of a range ring marker oscillator generating range rings at 10 nautical miles intervals?
explanation: Radar range time is 12.34 µs per nautical mile, so T = 10 × 12.34 µs = 123.4 µs and f = 1 / 123.4 µs ≈ 8.1 kHz, about 8 kHz.

stem: What is the distance between range markers if the controlling oscillator is operating at 20 kHz?
explanation: T = 1 / 20 kHz = 50 µs; range = 50 µs ÷ 12.34 µs per nautical mile ≈ 4.05, so about 4 nautical miles between markers.

stem: What would be the frequency of a range ring marker oscillator generating range rings at intervals of 0.25 nautical miles?
explanation: Ring spacing time is T = 0.25 × 12.34 µs = 3.085 µs, and f = 1 / T ≈ 324 kHz. The exam's 322 kHz figure evidently comes from rounding the period to 3.1 µs: f = 1 / 3.1 µs ≈ 322 kHz, the closest listed value.

stem: The variable range marker signal is normally fed to the input of the:
explanation: The VRM pulse is mixed with the echo video in the video amplifier so it appears on the display as a ring, just like the fixed range rings. The sweep amplifier handles only deflection drive.

stem: The purpose of the variable range marker is to:
choices: Provide an accurate means of determining the range of a moving target.
Provide a bearing line between own ship and a moving target.
Indicate the distance between two different targets.
Provide a means of calibrating the fixed range rings.
explanation: The VRM is a single ring the operator moves out until it touches a target's echo, then reads the range from its readout. It gives a far more precise range than estimating between fixed rings and is easily readjusted as a moving target's range changes.

stem: How is the variable range marker usually adjusted for accuracy?
choices: Adjusting the frequency of the VRM oscillator at the maximum range.
Adjusting the frequency of the VRM oscillator at the minimum range.
Adjusting the readout to match at the median range ring.
The minimum and maximum ranges are aligned with the matching fixed range ring.
explanation: VRM calibration checks both ends of its travel: at the minimum and maximum settings the VRM is adjusted to line up exactly with the matching fixed range rings, which serve as the accurate reference.

stem: The panel control for the variable range marker is normally a:
explanation: The VRM panel control is normally a potentiometer. Turning it changes a DC voltage that sets the marker's delay after the transmit pulse, moving the ring in or out.

stem: An important component of the VRM system is the:
explanation: In digital VRM circuits, a shift register (or counter chain) steps clock pulses after each transmit trigger and generates the marker after a precisely set delay, and that delay sets the ring's range.

stem: Which of the following statements about the Variable Range Marker system is correct?
choices: The VRM is an auxiliary output of the fixed range marker oscillator.
The VRM system develops a single adjustable range ring.
The VRM system is calibrated using a frequency counter.
The VRM system is controlled by a crystal oscillator.
explanation: The VRM produces one ring whose radius the operator adjusts to match a target's range. It is generated separately from the fixed range marker oscillator and is calibrated against the fixed rings rather than with a frequency counter.

stem: The purpose of the Electronic Bearing Line is to:
choices: Measure the bearing of a specific target.
Display the range of a specific target.
